questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 58-year-old man with a history of anterior wall MI 2 years ago presents with progressive exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, and bilateral pedal edema. His BP is 100/70 mmHg, HR 92/min, JVP elevated 5 cm above sternal angle, and S3 gallop is heard. LVEF on echocardiography is 30%. He is already on furosemide 40 mg/day. Which of the following combinations represents the MOST EVIDENCE-BASED pharmacological strategy to reduce mortality in this patient?

options.A: Add digoxin + spironolactone; digoxin reduces mortality and spironolactone improves symptoms
options.B: Add sacubitril-valsartan + carvedilol + spironolactone; this combination targets neurohormonal activation and has proven mortality benefit in HFrEF
options.C: Increase furosemide to 80 mg/day + add amlodipine; aggressive diuresis and afterload reduction are the cornerstones of HFrEF management
options.D: Add ivabradine alone; HR reduction is the single most important intervention in post-MI heart failure with reduced EF

questions.explanation: Correct (B): HFrEF (EF <40%) with post-MI etiology — evidence-based mortality-reducing therapy includes: (1) ACEi/ARB or ARNI (sacubitril-valsartan — PARADIGM-HF trial showed 20% reduction in CV death/HF hospitalization vs enalapril); (2) Beta-blocker (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol — COPERNICUS, MERIT-HF trials); (3) MRA (spironolactone/eplerenone — RALES trial: 30% mortality reduction; EMPHASIS-HF for eplerenone); (4) SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin/empagliflozin — DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-Reduced). This is the 'fantastic four' of HFrEF. BP 100/70 is acceptable for initiating these at low doses. Incorrect: (A) Digoxin reduces hospitalizations but does NOT reduce mortality (DIG trial); not first-line; (C) Amlodipine (dihydropyridine CCB) is neutral in HF — not contraindicated but provides no mortality benefit; aggressive diuresis alone doesn't reduce mortality; (D) Ivabradine (SHIFT trial) reduces HF hospitalization in patients with SR + HR ≥70 despite beta-blocker — beneficial but not the primary intervention and not used alone. Exam pearl: 'Fantastic Four' of HFrEF: ARNI + Beta-blocker + MRA + SGLT2i. Sacubitril-valsartan = FIRST choice over ACEi if patient can tolerate (36-hour washout required when switching from ACEi to avoid angioedema).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 42-year-old woman, 3 weeks post-cesarean section, presents with sudden onset dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and hemoptysis. HR 118/min, BP 94/60 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 86% on room air. ECG shows S1Q3T3 pattern and new right bundle branch block. CTPA confirms bilateral massive pulmonary embolism. Echocardiography shows right ventricular dilation with D-shaped septum. What is the MOST APPROPRIATE immediate management?

options.A: Start LMWH (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC BD) and admit to ICU; systemic thrombolysis is contraindicated within 6 weeks of surgery
options.B: Systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours is the treatment of choice for massive PE with hemodynamic compromise, with recent surgery as a relative (not absolute) contraindication
options.C: Start unfractionated heparin infusion only; massive PE with hypotension is managed conservatively with anticoagulation alone
options.D: Immediate surgical embolectomy is the only option as thrombolysis is absolutely contraindicated post-cesarean and anticoagulation is insufficient

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Massive PE = PE + sustained hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg or drop >40 mmHg for >15 min not due to other cause). This patient has hemodynamic compromise (BP 94/60), RV dysfunction (echo findings), and hypoxia — high mortality without reperfusion. Systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg/2hr) is the treatment of choice for massive PE. Recent surgery (<3 weeks absolute contraindication; 3 weeks to 3 months = RELATIVE contraindication) — at 3 weeks post-cesarean, this is a relative contraindication. In massive PE with life-threatening hemodynamic compromise, the risk-benefit FAVORS thrombolysis despite relative contraindications. If thrombolysis truly contraindicated → surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy. Incorrect: (A) LMWH alone = appropriate for submassive/low-risk PE; insufficient for massive PE with shock; (C) Anticoagulation alone is insufficient for massive PE — it prevents further clot but doesn't dissolve existing clot rapidly enough; (D) Recent surgery is a RELATIVE not absolute contraindication to thrombolysis; surgical embolectomy is second-line when thrombolysis fails or is absolutely contraindicated. Exam pearl: Massive PE = thrombolysis (alteplase). Submassive PE (RV dysfunction, no hypotension) = anticoagulation ± thrombolysis (controversial). S1Q3T3 = classic but insensitive ECG finding; sinus tachycardia is most common ECG change in PE.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 65-year-old hypertensive diabetic male is started on ramipril for proteinuria. Two weeks later, his creatinine rises from 1.1 to 1.8 mg/dL and potassium from 4.2 to 5.8 mEq/L. He has no other symptoms. Renal ultrasound shows both kidneys of normal size with increased echogenicity. Doppler study reveals bilateral renal artery stenosis (>70% bilaterally). What is the MOST APPROPRIATE next step?

options.A: Continue ramipril and add furosemide to manage the hyperkalemia; the creatinine rise is acceptable up to 30%
options.B: Stop ramipril immediately; ACEi/ARB are contraindicated in bilateral RAS as they remove the efferent arteriolar constriction maintaining GFR, causing acute-on-chronic kidney injury
options.C: Switch from ramipril to losartan; ARBs are safe in bilateral RAS whereas ACEi are not
options.D: Perform emergency renal angioplasty; bilateral RAS with AKI requires urgent revascularization before any pharmacological management

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Bilateral renal artery stenosis (or RAS in a solitary functioning kidney) is a CONTRAINDICATION to ACEi/ARB. Mechanism: In RAS, GFR is maintained by angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction. ACEi/ARB block Ang II → efferent vasodilation → drop in intraglomerular pressure → acute fall in GFR → AKI. Rise in creatinine >30% after starting ACEi = bilateral RAS until proven otherwise. Hyperkalemia compounds the danger. Action: STOP ACEi/ARB immediately. After stabilization, investigate and consider revascularization (angioplasty) if functionally significant. Incorrect: (A) Continuing is dangerous; a 64% rise in creatinine (1.1→1.8) in bilateral RAS warrants stopping, not continuing; the 30% acceptable rise rule applies to unilateral/non-stenotic scenarios; (C) ARBs have the SAME mechanism as ACEi — both block the RAAS efferent arteriolar effect — equally contraindicated in bilateral RAS; (D) Revascularization may be considered electively but is NOT the immediate next step before stopping the causative agent. Exam pearl: Bilateral RAS or RAS in solitary kidney = absolute contraindication to ACEi/ARB. 'ACEi + bilateral RAS = flash pulmonary edema risk + AKI.' RAAS blockade is beneficial in UNIlateral RAS with contralateral normal kidney.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 32-year-old woman presents with palpitations, heat intolerance, weight loss despite increased appetite, and diarrhea for 3 months. She has a diffusely enlarged smooth goiter and bilateral proptosis. TSH is undetectable, free T4 is 4.2 ng/dL (high), and TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb) are strongly positive. She is 10 weeks pregnant. Which of the following is the MOST APPROPRIATE management?

options.A: Radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy; it is the definitive treatment for Graves' disease and can be used safely in the first trimester
options.B: Propylthiouracil (PTU) in the first trimester; switch to methimazole after first trimester; avoid RAI in pregnancy
options.C: Methimazole throughout pregnancy; it is the preferred antithyroid drug due to lower risk of agranulocytosis
options.D: Total thyroidectomy in the second trimester; surgery is the only safe definitive option in pregnancy as both antithyroid drugs cause fetal malformations

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Graves' disease in pregnancy requires antithyroid drugs (ATDs). The choice changes by trimester: FIRST TRIMESTER → PTU preferred (methimazole associated with aplasia cutis, choanal atresia, esophageal atresia — 'methimazole embryopathy'); SECOND/THIRD TRIMESTER → switch to methimazole (PTU has risk of maternal hepatotoxicity with prolonged use — severe hepatitis, liver failure). Both cross placenta and can cause fetal hypothyroidism — use lowest effective dose. Target maternal fT4 at upper limit of normal. RAI is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy (destroys fetal thyroid from 10–12 weeks onward). Incorrect: (A) RAI = ABSOLUTELY contraindicated in pregnancy; fetal thyroid takes up iodine from 10–12 weeks → permanent fetal hypothyroidism; (C) Methimazole throughout pregnancy ignores the first-trimester teratogenicity risk; PTU is preferred in T1; (D) Both PTU and MMI are safe with careful monitoring; surgery (thyroidectomy) is SECOND LINE — reserved for allergy/non-compliance with ATDs; if needed, safest in 2nd trimester. Exam pearl: 'PTU in T1, MMI in T2/T3.' RAI = absolute CI in pregnancy. PTU blocks T4→T3 conversion (additional benefit). Both PTU and MMI can cause agranulocytosis — warn patients to report sore throat/fever.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 52-year-old male with known alcohol-related liver cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C) is admitted with massive hematemesis. On examination: BP 80/50 mmHg, HR 124/min, pallor, spider nevi, and splenomegaly. He is resuscitated with IV fluids. Upper GI endoscopy confirms grade III esophageal varices with active bleeding. After initial hemostasis with band ligation, which of the following is the MOST APPROPRIATE combination of pharmacological agents to reduce risk of rebleeding and prevent infection?

options.A: IV pantoprazole + sucralfate; acid suppression is the cornerstone of variceal bleed management
options.B: IV terlipressin (or octreotide/somatostatin) started before endoscopy + IV ceftriaxone for 5–7 days; vasoactive drugs + prophylactic antibiotics reduce mortality in acute variceal bleed
options.C: IV propranolol + oral rifaximin; beta-blocker reduces portal pressure and rifaximin prevents hepatic encephalopathy
options.D: Oral propranolol + spironolactone; non-selective beta-blocker is the only proven pharmacological agent for acute variceal hemorrhage

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Acute variceal hemorrhage management protocol: (1) VASOACTIVE DRUGS (start BEFORE endoscopy, continue 2–5 days): terlipressin (V1 agonist; only drug proven to reduce mortality — Baveno guidelines); alternatives = octreotide, somatostatin, vasopressin. Mechanism: splanchnic vasoconstriction → reduced portal pressure → controls bleeding. (2) PROPHYLACTIC ANTIBIOTICS: IV ceftriaxone 1g/day for 5–7 days (SBP prophylaxis + reduces bacterial translocation that drives rebleeding + reduces mortality — RCTs proven); oral norfloxacin is alternative. (3) Endoscopic band ligation (EBL) = gold standard hemostasis. (4) After stabilization: NSBB (propranolol/carvedilol) for secondary prophylaxis. Incorrect: (A) PPIs have NO role in variceal bleed (relevant for peptic ulcer bleed); sucralfate = peptic disease; (C) IV propranolol is not used acutely; beta-blockers are for secondary prophylaxis, not acute management; rifaximin = hepatic encephalopathy prophylaxis/treatment, not primary variceal bleed; (D) Spironolactone = ascites management; propranolol is for secondary prophylaxis, not acute bleed. Exam pearl: Baveno VII: Terlipressin + antibiotics + EBL = standard of care. Terlipressin CI in ischemic heart disease/peripheral vascular disease. TIPS = rescue therapy when endoscopy fails. Blood transfusion target Hb 7–8 g/dL (restrictive strategy) in variceal bleed — overtransfusion raises portal pressure.

questions.question_text: A 38-year-old woman presents with 8 months of bilateral symmetrical painful swelling of MCP and PIP joints, morning stiffness lasting >2 hours, and fatigue. The X-ray of her hands is shown. RF is positive (1:320), anti-CCP antibodies are strongly positive, CRP 48 mg/L, ESR 78 mm/hr. She has no prior treatment. Which of the following represents the MOST APPROPRIATE initial DMARD strategy?

options.A: Hydroxychloroquine monotherapy; it is the safest DMARD with fewest side effects and is first-line for all RA
options.B: Methotrexate (MTX) as the anchor DMARD, typically combined with short-term bridging corticosteroids; MTX is the gold standard first-line DMARD for RA
options.C: Immediate biologic therapy (adalimumab); anti-CCP positivity with erosions mandates upfront TNF-alpha inhibitor
options.D: Sulfasalazine monotherapy; it is preferred over methotrexate in seropositive RA with erosive disease

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Methotrexate (MTX) is the ANCHOR DMARD and gold standard first-line therapy for RA regardless of serostatus. Benefits: proven disease modification, erosion prevention, mortality reduction. Dose: 10–25 mg/week + folic acid 1–5 mg/day (reduces toxicity). Bridging with low-dose prednisolone (or IM methylprednisolone) while awaiting MTX onset (6–8 weeks). Strong evidence supports MTX as first-line in ACR/EULAR guidelines. Anti-CCP positivity predicts erosive disease but does NOT mandate upfront biologics — biologics (TNF-alpha inhibitors, etc.) are second-line after inadequate response to conventional DMARDs. Incorrect: (A) Hydroxychloroquine is used in mild/early RA or as add-on therapy; NOT first-line for erosive seropositive RA; (C) Biologic therapy is second-line (after failure of ≥1 csDMARD); not upfront for newly diagnosed RA even with erosions and seropositivity (cost, infection risk, guidelines); (D) Sulfasalazine is an alternative first-line csDMARD (particularly if MTX contraindicated) but NOT preferred over MTX in erosive seropositive disease. Exam pearl: MTX side effects: hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs), pulmonary toxicity (MTX pneumonitis), bone marrow suppression, mucositis. CONTRAINDICATIONS: pregnancy (teratogenic — category X), significant renal impairment, hepatic disease, alcohol use. Treat-to-target: aim for remission or low disease activity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 68-year-old man with hypertension and atrial fibrillation presents with sudden onset right-sided hemiplegia and aphasia. Onset was 2.5 hours ago. NIHSS score is 14. Non-contrast CT head shows no hemorrhage and no early ischemic changes. BP 178/96 mmHg. His current medications include warfarin (INR today = 1.3). What is the MOST APPROPRIATE immediate management?

options.A: IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg) immediately; INR 1.3 is below the cut-off of 1.7, and he is within the thrombolysis window
options.B: Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) alone without thrombolysis; MT is now first-line for all strokes and thrombolysis is outdated
options.C: Withhold thrombolysis due to warfarin use; start aspirin 300 mg and admit for observation; anticoagulation can be restarted after 2 weeks
options.D: IV alteplase + CT angiography; if large vessel occlusion confirmed, proceed to mechanical thrombectomy (bridging approach)

questions.explanation: Correct (D): This is an acute ischemic stroke with NIHSS 14 (moderate-severe), within 4.5-hour thrombolysis window, no hemorrhage on CT, and INR 1.3 (<1.7 = thrombolysis permissible despite warfarin). Standard approach: (1) IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg; 10% bolus, rest over 60 min) — if no contraindications; (2) Simultaneously perform CTA to identify large vessel occlusion (LVO — MCA/ICA/basilar); (3) If LVO confirmed → proceed to mechanical thrombectomy (MT); bridging IV thrombolysis + MT is standard for eligible patients with LVO within 6 hours (DAWN/DEFUSE-3 up to 24 hours with imaging criteria). The two therapies are complementary, not mutually exclusive. INR cut-off for thrombolysis: ≤1.7. Incorrect: (A) Correct about INR but incomplete — CTA for LVO and potential thrombectomy should be done simultaneously; (B) MT is first-line for LVO but does not replace thrombolysis in eligible patients — guidelines recommend bridging; MT alone is used when thrombolysis is contraindicated; (C) INR 1.3 is BELOW the cut-off of 1.7 — warfarin use alone does NOT contraindicate thrombolysis here; aspirin alone is insufficient for this severity. Exam pearl: Thrombolysis contraindications: INR >1.7, platelets <100k, prior ICH, current major surgery <14 days, BP >185/110 (treatable). Time = brain: 1.9 million neurons lost per minute in stroke. 'Time is Brain.'

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old HIV-positive male (CD4 count 85 cells/μL, on ART for 3 months) is started on anti-TB therapy (HRZE) for pulmonary TB. Three weeks later he develops high-grade fever, worsening respiratory symptoms, new lymphadenopathy, and a new pleural effusion despite compliance with both ART and ATT. Sputum AFB smear is negative. What is the MOST LIKELY diagnosis and the APPROPRIATE management?

options.A: Drug-resistant TB (MDR-TB); send sputum for CBNAAT/culture and DST; switch to second-line anti-TB drugs empirically
options.B: Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS); continue both ART and ATT; add NSAIDs or corticosteroids for severe symptoms; do not stop ART
options.C: ART drug toxicity causing drug reaction with eosinophilia; stop ART and substitute offending agent; continue ATT
options.D: Paradoxical TB progression; stop ART to reduce immune activation; TB-IRIS does not occur in patients with CD4 >50

questions.explanation: Correct (B): TB-IRIS (Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome) — paradoxical type: occurs when ART is started in a patient already on ATT (or TB diagnosed simultaneously) → as CD4 count recovers, immune system mounts exaggerated inflammatory response to TB antigens → paradoxical worsening of TB despite effective treatment. Risk factors: low baseline CD4 (<100), high baseline TB burden, early ART initiation (<2 weeks of ATT). Features: fever, worsening lymphadenopathy, new/worsening pulmonary infiltrates, pleural effusions, new organ involvement — all 3 weeks after ART start in this case. Management: (1) Continue BOTH ART and ATT (do NOT stop); (2) Exclude drug resistance and opportunistic infections first; (3) NSAIDs for mild IRIS; (4) Prednisolone 1–1.5 mg/kg/day for moderate-severe IRIS (evidence: STRIDE/SAPiT trial). Incorrect: (A) MDR-TB should be excluded (CBNAAT) but clinical picture here — temporal relationship to ART initiation, negative smear, no prior TB treatment — strongly suggests IRIS rather than MDR; (C) ART toxicity doesn't explain new TB manifestations; (D) ART must NOT be stopped — stopping worsens HIV disease; IRIS can occur at any CD4 count, more common at <100. Exam pearl: IRIS = worsening despite effective treatment + temporal relationship to ART/immunotherapy. Timing: 2–12 weeks after ART initiation. Never stop ART for IRIS (only life-threatening central nervous system IRIS may require temporary ART interruption in rare cases).

questions.question_text: A 55-year-old vegetarian woman presents with progressive weakness, paresthesia in hands and feet, and difficulty walking for 6 months. She has a past history of autoimmune thyroid disease. CBC shows Hb 7.2 g/dL, MCV 118 fL, WBC 3.2 × 10⁹/L, platelets 98 × 10⁹/L. Serum B12 is 82 pg/mL (low). Peripheral smear is shown. Bone marrow shows megaloblastic changes. Serum methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are both elevated. The MOST LIKELY underlying cause and the MOST APPROPRIATE treatment is:

options.A: Dietary B12 deficiency due to strict vegetarianism; treat with oral cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg/day indefinitely
options.B: Pernicious anemia (autoimmune gastritis with anti-intrinsic factor antibodies); treat with IM hydroxocobalamin 1000 mcg on alternate days for 2 weeks, then monthly for life
options.C: Folate deficiency; treat with oral folic acid 5 mg/day; B12 levels are misleadingly low due to folate trap
options.D: Hemolytic anemia with B12 deficiency; bone marrow biopsy is needed before starting treatment to exclude myelodysplastic syndrome

questions.explanation: Correct (B): This is PERNICIOUS ANEMIA — classic triad: (1) Megaloblastic anemia; (2) Neurological features (subacute combined degeneration of cord — paresthesia, ataxia, posterior column + lateral column involvement); (3) Autoimmune background (thyroid disease, vitiligo, Addison's — associated). Pathophysiology: autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells → loss of intrinsic factor → failure of B12 absorption in terminal ileum. Elevated methylmalonic acid AND homocysteine = B12 deficiency confirmed (folate deficiency elevates only homocysteine, NOT MMA). Hypersegmented neutrophils + macro-ovalocytes = megaloblastic anemia on smear. Treatment: IM hydroxocobalamin (bypasses GI absorption defect): 1000 mcg on alternate days × 2 weeks (loading), then monthly for life. Intrinsic factor antibodies/parietal cell antibodies confirm pernicious anemia. Incorrect: (A) Pure dietary deficiency = oral supplementation works; but pernicious anemia requires IM (oral absorption bypassed by IF defect); (C) Folate deficiency does NOT elevate MMA; neurological features = B12, not folate; treating with folate alone can worsen neurological damage by correcting anemia while B12 deficiency continues; (D) MDS should be excluded in elderly patients but this clinical picture + B12 level is diagnostic; treatment should not be delayed. Exam pearl: B12 deficiency = elevated MCV + elevated MMA + elevated homocysteine + hypersegmented neutrophils + neuropsychiatric features. Folate deficiency = elevated MCV + elevated homocysteine ONLY (normal MMA). Never give folate alone without B12 in combined deficiency — risks neurological catastrophe.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man presents with severe crushing chest pain, diaphoresis, and nausea of 90-minute duration. BP 88/60 mmHg, HR 48/min, JVP elevated with Kussmaul's sign, lungs are clear, and there is right-sided S3. The ECG is shown. Right-sided ECG leads show ST elevation in V4R. What is the MOST LIKELY diagnosis and the MOST CRITICAL management consideration?

options.A: Anterior STEMI with cardiogenic shock; urgent PCI; give IV furosemide for elevated JVP and start dobutamine
options.B: Inferior STEMI with right ventricular infarction; urgent primary PCI; AVOID nitrates and diuretics — preload-dependent state; IV fluids for hypotension
options.C: Inferior STEMI without RV involvement; nitrates and morphine are safe; elevated JVP indicates left heart failure requiring diuresis
options.D: NSTEMI with acute pericarditis; start aspirin + colchicine; urgent PCI not indicated as there is no true ST elevation

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Inferior STEMI (ST elevation in II, III, aVF) with RIGHT VENTRICULAR INFARCTION (ST elevation in V4R on right-sided leads). RV infarction = classically occurs with right coronary artery (RCA) occlusion causing inferior STEMI. Clinical triad of RV infarction: (1) Hypotension (BP 88/60); (2) Elevated JVP (Kussmaul's sign — JVP rises on inspiration); (3) Clear lung fields (no pulmonary edema — RV failure without LV involvement). RV infarction = PRELOAD DEPENDENT (RV needs adequate filling pressure to maintain output). CRITICAL: AVOID nitrates (reduce preload → severe hypotension, can be fatal) and diuretics. Treatment: IV fluid loading (NS 200 mL boluses) to maintain preload, primary PCI of RCA, inotropes (dobutamine) if no response to fluids. ST depression in V1–V3 = posterior MI component. Incorrect: (A) Anterior STEMI would show V1–V4 ST elevation; furosemide is HARMFUL in RV infarction; (C) Nitrates are CONTRAINDICATED in RV infarction — can cause severe hypotension; elevated JVP here is from RV failure, not LV failure; (D) This is clearly STEMI (>2 mm elevation in 2 contiguous inferior leads); no saddle-shape diffuse changes of pericarditis. Exam pearl: 'RV infarction = Hypotension + Elevated JVP + Clear lungs.' V4R ST elevation ≥1 mm = pathognomonic of RV MI. 'Nitrates KILL in RV MI.' RCA = 70% of inferior MIs. Always obtain right-sided ECG in inferior STEMI.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old male with type 2 DM (HbA1c 9.2%), hypertension, and established ASCVD (prior MI 1 year ago) is on metformin 2g/day, sitagliptin 100 mg/day, and glimepiride 4 mg/day. His eGFR is 52 mL/min/1.73m². He has no heart failure. Which modification to his antidiabetic regimen would provide the MOST BENEFIT in terms of cardiovascular outcomes?

options.A: Add pioglitazone; TZDs reduce HbA1c effectively and have proven cardiovascular benefit in patients with prior MI
options.B: Add empagliflozin (SGLT2 inhibitor); proven reduction in MACE, CV death, and HF hospitalization in patients with established ASCVD (EMPA-REG OUTCOME trial); eGFR 52 permits use
options.C: Switch sitagliptin to saxagliptin; saxagliptin has superior cardiovascular outcomes compared to other DPP-4 inhibitors in post-MI patients
options.D: Add insulin glargine; intensive glycemic control with insulin is the only proven strategy to reduce CV events in T2DM with prior MI

questions.explanation: Correct (B): In T2DM with ESTABLISHED ASCVD (prior MI), the priority after metformin is adding a drug with proven CV benefit: (1) SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin — EMPA-REG OUTCOME; canagliflozin — CANVAS; dapagliflozin — DECLARE-TIMI): reduce MACE, CV death, HF hospitalizations; empagliflozin showed 38% reduction in CV death. (2) GLP-1 RAs (liraglutide — LEADER; semaglutide — SUSTAIN-6): reduce MACE, particularly atherosclerotic events. eGFR 52 mL/min: SGLT2 inhibitors are used down to eGFR 20 (empagliflozin/dapagliflozin for HF/CKD benefit), and for glycemic benefit down to eGFR 30–45 depending on drug. Empagliflozin is appropriate here. Glimepiride (sulfonylurea) should ideally be deprioritized (hypoglycemia risk, weight gain, no CV benefit). Incorrect: (A) Pioglitazone — PROactive trial showed some CV benefit (secondary endpoint) but it causes fluid retention, heart failure, bladder cancer, fractures; NOT first-line add-on in ASCVD with prior MI; (C) Saxagliptin (SAVOR-TIMI) showed INCREASED HF hospitalization — should be used cautiously, particularly avoided in HF; DPP-4 inhibitors are CV-neutral overall, not superior; (D) ACCORD trial: intensive glycemic control with insulin did not reduce CV events and increased mortality in high-risk T2DM. Exam pearl: ASCVD + T2DM: prefer SGLT2i or GLP-1RA after metformin. HF + T2DM: SGLT2i (dapagliflozin — DAPA-HF; empagliflozin — EMPEROR-Reduced). CKD + T2DM: SGLT2i (CREDENCE, DAPA-CKD).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 24-year-old man presents with 2 weeks of gross hematuria (tea-colored urine), facial puffiness, and oliguria following a sore throat 2 weeks ago. BP 158/96 mmHg. Urinalysis: RBC casts, proteinuria 2+ (800 mg/day). C3 is markedly reduced, C4 is normal. ASO titer is elevated. Renal biopsy shows diffuse endocapillary proliferation with 'humps' (subepithelial deposits) on electron microscopy and granular IgG + C3 deposits on immunofluorescence. What is the MOST LIKELY diagnosis and its expected prognosis in adults?

options.A: IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease); hematuria following pharyngitis, low C3, and mesangial IgA deposits; prognosis is generally excellent with complete recovery
options.B: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN); excellent prognosis in children; in adults, prognosis is less favorable with up to 50% developing persistent renal dysfunction or hypertension
options.C: Lupus nephritis class III; C3 reduction, immune complex deposits; renal biopsy mandatory; aggressive immunosuppression required
options.D: Membranoproliferative GN type I; C3 reduction with C4 reduction, mesangial deposits; prognosis is poor universally

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Post-streptococcal GN (PSGN) — classic presentation: latent period of 1–3 weeks after pharyngitis (10–21 days) or 3–6 weeks after impetigo → nephritic syndrome (hematuria, oliguria, hypertension, RBC casts, mild-moderate proteinuria). Diagnostics: low C3 (classical pathway activation), NORMAL C4 (alternative pathway primarily), elevated ASO/anti-DNase B. Biopsy: 'starry sky' pattern — diffuse endocapillary proliferation; 'humps' = subepithelial immune complex deposits (electron microscopy); granular IgG + C3 on IF ('lumpy bumpy'). Prognosis: CHILDREN: >95% complete recovery. ADULTS: significantly worse — 25–50% may develop persistent proteinuria, hypertension, or progressive CKD. Treatment: supportive (antihypertensives, salt/fluid restriction, loop diuretics); antibiotics if active streptococcal infection; NO immunosuppression. Incorrect: (A) IgA nephropathy = hematuria 1–3 days after pharyngitis (synpharyngitic); NORMAL complement; mesangial IgA deposits; NOT subepithelial 'humps'; (C) Lupus nephritis = C3 AND C4 low; ANA/anti-dsDNA positive; multiorganism involvement; (D) MPGN type I = C3 AND C4 low; tram-track appearance on LM; mesangial and subendothelial deposits. Exam pearl: PSGN: C3 low, C4 normal. SLE nephritis: C3 AND C4 low. MPGN type I: C3 and C4 low. Dense deposit disease (MPGN type II): C3 very low, C4 normal (C3 nephritic factor). Latency = key: 10–21 days (pharyngitis) vs 3–6 weeks (skin). 'Humps' = PSGN.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 65-year-old male smoker (45 pack-years) presents with worsening dyspnea on exertion and chronic productive cough for 10 years. Spirometry post-bronchodilator: FEV1/FVC = 0.58, FEV1 = 48% predicted. He has 2 exacerbations requiring hospitalization in the past year and current CAT score of 22. He is on salbutamol as needed. According to GOLD 2023 guidelines, which treatment strategy is MOST APPROPRIATE for long-term maintenance?

options.A: Add inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) monotherapy (fluticasone); ICS alone is recommended for high-exacerbation-risk COPD
options.B: Long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) + Long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) combination (e.g., indacaterol + glycopyrronium); dual bronchodilation is preferred for symptomatic patients with high exacerbation risk
options.C: LABA + LAMA + ICS triple therapy (e.g., budesonide/glycopyrronium/formoterol); indicated for this patient given high symptom burden, GOLD stage 3, and ≥2 hospitalizations
options.D: Oral theophylline + systemic corticosteroids; oral agents are more effective than inhalers in severe COPD with frequent exacerbations

questions.explanation: Correct (C): GOLD 2023 classification: FEV1 48% = GOLD Stage 3 (severe); Group E (≥2 exacerbations/year or ≥1 hospitalization = high exacerbation risk) + CAT ≥10 (high symptoms). Management for Group E (high risk): GOLD recommends LABA + LAMA as initial therapy; if blood eosinophils ≥300/μL or frequent exacerbations on LABA+LAMA, ADD ICS → triple therapy. This patient: 2 hospitalizations + CAT 22 + GOLD stage 3 = high risk; trial of LABA+LAMA first, but given severity and exacerbation burden, LABA+LAMA+ICS triple therapy (IMPACT trial, ETHOS trial: reduced exacerbations and mortality with triple) is the most appropriate maintenance strategy. ICS benefit in COPD is linked to blood eosinophil count (≥300 = good response). Incorrect: (A) ICS monotherapy is NOT recommended in COPD (unlike asthma) — causes infections without proven benefit alone; (B) LABA+LAMA dual is appropriate for Group E initial therapy but given the severe exacerbation history and symptom burden, triple therapy is more appropriate for this stage; (D) Oral theophylline = narrow therapeutic index, multiple drug interactions, modest benefit; NOT preferred; systemic corticosteroids = long-term oral steroids are avoided in COPD maintenance (only for acute exacerbations). Exam pearl: GOLD 2023 pivoted from ABCD to ABE groups. Triple therapy (LABA+LAMA+ICS): IMPACT trial — significant reduction in exacerbations. Check eosinophils before adding ICS — ≥300 = good ICS response.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old man with known Crohn's disease (ileocolonic, inflammatory phenotype, on azathioprine 2.5 mg/kg/day for 18 months) presents with 6 weeks of worsening abdominal pain, diarrhea (6–8 stools/day with blood), weight loss of 8 kg, CRP 78 mg/L, fecal calprotectin 1800 μg/g, and albumin 2.6 g/dL. Colonoscopy shows deep linear ulcers with cobblestoning in the terminal ileum and ascending colon. Harvey-Bradshaw Index = 14 (severe). He has failed to respond to a further course of prednisolone. What is the MOST APPROPRIATE next management step?

options.A: Increase azathioprine dose to 3 mg/kg/day; inadequate dosing is the most likely cause of treatment failure; check TPMT enzyme activity
options.B: Add methotrexate to azathioprine; combination immunomodulator therapy is the next step before considering biologics
options.C: Switch to anti-TNF therapy (infliximab or adalimumab); patient has steroid-refractory severe Crohn's disease who has failed immunomodulator; biologic therapy is indicated
options.D: Emergency surgical resection; severe Crohn's disease with albumin <3 g/dL mandates immediate surgical intervention without attempting biologic therapy

questions.explanation: Correct (C): This patient has STEROID-REFRACTORY, IMMUNOMODULATOR-FAILED severe Crohn's disease — classic indication for biologic therapy. Step-up approach: 5-ASA → immunomodulators (AZA/6-MP/MTX) → biologics (anti-TNF: infliximab IV or adalimumab SC). Anti-TNF therapy (infliximab — ACCENT I trial; adalimumab — CHARM trial) induces and maintains remission in moderate-severe Crohn's. Infliximab is preferred for severe/hospitalized patients (IV loading). Additional considerations: screen for TB (Mantoux/IGRA) + hepatitis B before starting anti-TNF; nutritional support (albumin 2.6 = hypoalbuminemia, poor healing). Vedolizumab or ustekinumab = alternatives if anti-TNF fails or contraindicated. Incorrect: (A) Increasing AZA above 2.5 mg/kg is not standard; check TPMT to assess metabolizer status but the clinical picture (18 months AZA + steroid failure) = inadequate response, not just underdosing; (B) Combination AZA + MTX is not standard (increased toxicity, no proven superiority); MTX alone is alternative to AZA, not add-on; (D) Surgery is NOT indicated here — no obstruction, perforation, abscess, or fistula; biologics should be tried first; surgery for Crohn's is not curative and has significant morbidity. Exam pearl: Crohn's biologics: infliximab (chimeric anti-TNF), adalimumab (fully human anti-TNF), vedolizumab (anti-integrin, gut-selective), ustekinumab (anti-IL-12/23). Always screen TB + HBV before anti-TNF. UC biologics: same anti-TNFs + tofacitinib (JAK inhibitor).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) is well-controlled on sodium valproate 1000 mg/day for 3 years. She is planning pregnancy in 6 months. Her neurologist is counseling her about AED management. Which of the following represents the MOST APPROPRIATE advice?

options.A: Continue valproate without change; seizure control during pregnancy is paramount and valproate is the most effective drug for JME
options.B: Switch to levetiracetam or lamotrigine before conception; valproate has the highest teratogenic risk of all AEDs (neural tube defects, cognitive impairment in offspring, fetal valproate syndrome); supplemental folic acid 5 mg/day recommended
options.C: Stop all AEDs immediately; risks to fetus outweigh benefits; JME seizures are rarely life-threatening and can be managed lifestyle alone
options.D: Switch to phenobarbitone; it is the oldest and most studied AED in pregnancy with established safety profile superior to valproate

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Sodium valproate in pregnancy: HIGHEST teratogenic risk among AEDs. Risks: (1) Neural tube defects (spina bifida) — 1–2% risk (10× general population); (2) Fetal valproate syndrome: craniofacial anomalies, limb defects; (3) Cognitive impairment in child (IQ reduction of 7–10 points — NEAD study); (4) Autism spectrum risk. EU/MHRA/FDA: valproate absolutely contraindicated in women of childbearing potential unless on pregnancy prevention program. IDEAL pre-conception switch: levetiracetam (safest pregnancy profile, Category C but reassuring data) OR lamotrigine (may need dose increase in pregnancy as levels drop). Note: lamotrigine less effective for myoclonic seizures — levetiracetam preferred for JME. High-dose folic acid 5 mg/day started pre-conception and continued through T1. Incorrect: (A) Continuing valproate in a woman planning pregnancy is now contra-indicated under MHRA/EU guidelines (PREVENT program); (C) Stopping all AEDs is dangerous — uncontrolled seizures cause maternal and fetal harm (SUDEP risk, trauma); (D) Phenobarbitone is teratogenic (cleft lip/palate, cardiac defects), associated with neonatal coagulation defects, and cognitive effects — NOT safer than valproate. Exam pearl: Valproate = highest teratogenicity. Safest AEDs in pregnancy: levetiracetam, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine (but all increase neural tube risk — folic acid 5 mg mandatory). Folic acid: 0.4 mg/day (general population), 5 mg/day (AED users, prior NTD, family history).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old male returns from sub-Saharan Africa with 5 days of high-grade fever with chills and rigors. He is confused, icteric, and has a palpable spleen. BP 90/60 mmHg, HR 116/min. Blood sugar is 40 mg/dL. Thick smear shows ring forms with multiple rings per RBC and 'banana-shaped' gametocytes. Parasitemia is 8%. Urine is cola-colored and hemoglobin is 6.2 g/dL. Serum creatinine is 3.4 mg/dL. What is the MOST APPROPRIATE immediate treatment?

options.A: Oral artemether-lumefantrine (Coartem) 4 tablets twice daily for 3 days; adequate for severe malaria as artemisinin combination therapy is now standard
options.B: IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 hours then daily; IV artesunate is the drug of choice for severe P. falciparum malaria; correct hypoglycemia with IV dextrose
options.C: IV quinine + doxycycline; quinine remains first-line for severe malaria as artesunate is unavailable in most settings; immediate exchange transfusion for parasitemia >5%
options.D: Intramuscular artemether 3.2 mg/kg loading dose; IM route is preferred over IV in severe malaria to avoid complications of IV therapy

questions.explanation: Correct (B): This is SEVERE P. falciparum malaria — criteria met: (1) Cerebral malaria (confusion/altered sensorium); (2) Severe anemia (Hb 6.2); (3) Acute kidney injury (Cr 3.4); (4) Hypoglycemia (glucose 40 mg/dL); (5) Hemoglobinuria ('blackwater fever' = massive hemolysis); (6) Parasitemia >5%. Treatment: IV ARTESUNATE — WHO and SEQUAMAT/AQUAMAT trials: IV artesunate superior to IV quinine (22% reduction in mortality). Dose: 2.4 mg/kg IV at 0, 12, 24 hours, then daily for minimum 24 hours; once patient can swallow — complete with oral ACT (artemether-lumefantrine) for 3 days. Concurrent management: IV dextrose (50%) for hypoglycemia, blood transfusion for severe anemia, fluid management for AKI, ICU care. Incorrect: (A) Oral ACT is for UNCOMPLICATED malaria — NOT for severe malaria with complications; altered sensorium precludes oral therapy; (C) IV quinine is SECOND-LINE (if artesunate unavailable); exchange transfusion is controversial and NOT routinely recommended by WHO (benefit unproven); (D) IM artemether is an alternative when IV artesunate is unavailable — but IV artesunate is superior and preferred when available. Exam pearl: Severe malaria criteria (WHO): altered consciousness, prostration, multiple convulsions, deep breathing/respiratory distress, abnormal bleeding, jaundice, hemoglobinuria, severe anemia (Hb <7), hyperparasitemia (>5%), AKI, hypoglycemia, hypotension, pulmonary edema. IV artesunate = drug of choice.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 26-year-old woman presents with 3 months of malar rash, oral ulcers, arthritis, pleuritis, and now presents with confusion and seizures. Investigations: Hb 9.2 g/dL (Coombs positive), WBC 2,800/μL, platelets 68,000/μL, creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, proteinuria 3.5 g/day, C3 and C4 both markedly low, ANA 1:1280 (homogeneous), anti-dsDNA strongly positive, anti-Sm positive. Urinalysis shows RBC casts. She is also found to have prolonged aPTT not correcting with mixing study, and anti-cardiolipin antibody (IgG) at 60 GPL units. What is the MOST COMPLETE and ACCURATE diagnosis and the MOST APPROPRIATE initial management?

options.A: SLE with class IV lupus nephritis; treat with IV methylprednisolone pulse + mycophenolate mofetil (MMF); no anticoagulation needed as aPTT prolongation is due to lupus anticoagulant artifact
options.B: SLE with class IV lupus nephritis + neuropsychiatric SLE (NPSLE) + secondary antiphospholipid syndrome (APS); pulse IV methylprednisolone + MMF/cyclophosphamide for nephritis; anticoagulation for APS; hydroxychloroquine as background therapy
options.C: Drug-induced lupus with renal involvement; stop the offending drug; short course of steroids is curative; APS antibodies are non-specific
options.D: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) presenting with SLE-like features; plasma exchange is the immediate priority; steroids are contraindicated

questions.explanation: Correct (B): This patient has SLE (ACR/EULAR criteria met: malar rash, oral ulcers, arthritis, serositis, nephritis, hematological — Coombs+ hemolytic anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm) PLUS: (1) CLASS IV LUPUS NEPHRITIS (diffuse — proteinuria 3.5g + RBC casts + AKI + low C3/C4); (2) NEUROPSYCHIATRIC SLE (confusion, seizures); (3) SECONDARY APS: anti-cardiolipin IgG high positive + lupus anticoagulant (prolonged aPTT not correcting on mixing = inhibitor = LA). Management: (a) Pulse IV methylprednisolone (1g/day × 3 days) → high-dose oral prednisolone; (b) Induction: MMF (2–3 g/day) or cyclophosphamide (Euro-Lupus protocol) for class IV; (c) Hydroxychloroquine 400 mg/day (reduces flares, organ damage, mortality — background therapy for ALL SLE); (d) Anticoagulation for APS (LMWH → warfarin; target INR 2–3 for venous thrombosis; 2.5–3.5 for arterial); (e) Belimumab (anti-BAFF) as add-on for refractory SLE. Incorrect: (A) Ignores NPSLE and APS — LA is not merely an artifact; APS requires treatment with anticoagulation to prevent thrombosis; (C) Drug-induced lupus: usually anti-histone antibodies, rarely causes nephritis, usually no anti-dsDNA; (D) TTP presents with MAHA + thrombocytopenia + neurological but RBC CASTS + massive proteinuria + positive ANA/anti-dsDNA = SLE nephritis is the primary diagnosis. Exam pearl: Anti-Sm = most specific for SLE. Anti-dsDNA = most specific + correlates with disease activity/nephritis. APS criteria: clinical (thrombosis/pregnancy morbidity) + antibody (LA/aCL/anti-β2GPI) on 2 occasions 12 weeks apart. Hydroxychloroquine = mandatory in all SLE patients (background therapy).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 22-year-old woman is brought to the emergency with 5 days of jaundice, nausea, and confusion (Grade II hepatic encephalopathy). No past history of liver disease. Total bilirubin 28 mg/dL, ALT 3240 U/L, INR 4.8, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL. She reportedly took 'a lot of paracetamol tablets' after a breakup 6 days ago. NAC (N-acetylcysteine) was not started. Serum paracetamol level is now undetectable. Should NAC still be given, and what is the MOST APPROPRIATE immediate management?

options.A: NAC is ineffective once paracetamol is undetectable; focus on liver transplant evaluation; start lactulose and rifaximin for encephalopathy
options.B: IV NAC should be started even with undetectable paracetamol levels — evidence (ALFSG trial) shows NAC improves transplant-free survival in ALL non-acetaminophen ALF and reduces organ failure; simultaneously evaluate for liver transplantation using King's College Criteria
options.C: Oral NAC 140 mg/kg loading then 70 mg/kg every 4 hours × 17 doses; oral route is preferred over IV as it achieves higher hepatic concentrations in established liver failure
options.D: Forced diuresis and urinary alkalinization to enhance paracetamol elimination; since drug level is undetectable, primary focus is on dialysis for AKI

questions.explanation: Correct (B): NAC in ALF (ALFSG trial — Lee et al., 2009): IV NAC improved transplant-free survival in NON-acetaminophen ALF (early encephalopathy grades I–II: survival benefit significant). Mechanism beyond paracetamol toxicity: NAC replenishes glutathione, improves mitochondrial function, microcirculatory benefits, anti-inflammatory. Even with undetectable paracetamol — NAC should be given in ALF of any cause (particularly early encephalopathy). Protocol: IV NAC (preferred in ALF over oral due to unreliable GI absorption and vomiting) — Rumack-Matthew protocol (21-hour IV protocol) OR prolonged infusion. King's College Criteria for liver transplant referral in paracetamol-induced ALF: pH <7.3 after resuscitation, OR all three: PT >100 sec + creatinine >3.4 + Grade III/IV encephalopathy. Additional management: treat encephalopathy (lactulose, rifaximin), manage AKI (fluids, consider RRT), treat hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, cerebral edema. Incorrect: (A) NAC has benefit in early encephalopathy (grades I–II) ALF even without detectable drug; not starting NAC is an error; (C) Oral NAC has unreliable absorption in liver failure (N/V, ileus); IV is preferred; (D) Forced diuresis/alkalinization = salicylate overdose management; not applicable here. Exam pearl: King's College Criteria: most widely used prognostic tool in ALF for transplant listing. Paracetamol: NAPQI (toxic metabolite) → glutathione depletion → centrilobular necrosis. N-acetylcysteine = glutathione precursor.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old African-American male with stage 2 hypertension (BP 158/96 mmHg on two readings), no diabetes, no CKD, and no heart failure presents for management. He has no compelling indications for a specific drug class. According to JNC 8 and ACC/AHA 2017 guidelines, which of the following is the MOST APPROPRIATE initial antihypertensive agent?

options.A: ACE inhibitor (ramipril); first-line for all hypertensive patients regardless of ethnicity
options.B: Beta-blocker (atenolol); preferred for stage 2 hypertension due to its cardiac protective effects
options.C: Thiazide diuretic (chlorthalidone) or calcium channel blocker (amlodipine); Black patients respond better to these due to low-renin hypertension; ACEi/ARBs less effective as monotherapy in this population
options.D: ARB (telmisartan); preferred over ACEi in all non-diabetic hypertensive patients to avoid cough

questions.explanation: Correct (C): African-American/Black patients with hypertension have predominantly LOW-RENIN hypertension — RAAS-blocking agents (ACEi/ARB) are LESS EFFECTIVE as monotherapy in this population. Preferred first-line agents: (1) THIAZIDE DIURETICS (chlorthalidone — preferred over HCTZ: longer half-life, better CV outcomes — ALLHAT trial); (2) CALCIUM CHANNEL BLOCKERS (amlodipine — ALLHAT trial supports CCB in Black patients). ALLHAT trial (largest antihypertensive trial): chlorthalidone = amlodipine > lisinopril in Black patients for stroke/CV outcomes. ACC/AHA 2017: for Black patients without CKD/HF/diabetes, prefer thiazide or CCB. If combination needed: CCB + thiazide or CCB + ACEi (second-line). Incorrect: (A) ACEi monotherapy is LESS effective in Black patients; preferred in diabetic nephropathy, heart failure, post-MI — not as first-line monotherapy in Black patients; (B) Beta-blockers are NOT first-line antihypertensives (JNC 8 downgraded BB from first-line); reserved for compelling indications (angina, HF, post-MI); (D) ARBs = same limitation as ACEi in Black patients (renin-dependent). Exam pearl: JNC 8 first-line in NON-Black: ACEi OR ARB OR CCB OR thiazide diuretic. In BLACK patients: CCB OR thiazide (NOT ACEi/ARB as monotherapy). Chlorthalidone > HCTZ (longer half-life, greater reduction in CV events).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 38-year-old woman presents with episodic hypertension (BP spikes to 220/130 mmHg), palpitations, severe headache, diaphoresis, and pallor occurring in paroxysms lasting 15–20 minutes. Between episodes BP is normal. Random plasma metanephrines are markedly elevated (4× upper limit of normal). CT abdomen shows a 4.2 cm right adrenal mass. What is the correct sequence of management BEFORE surgical resection?

options.A: Proceed directly to laparoscopic adrenalectomy; surgery should not be delayed in hypertensive crisis; phenoxybenzamine causes rebound hypertension postoperatively
options.B: Start alpha-blocker (phenoxybenzamine) first for 10–14 days, then add beta-blocker ONLY after adequate alpha-blockade; IV fluids and high-salt diet to expand volume; then surgery
options.C: Start beta-blocker (propranolol) first to control heart rate and palpitations, then add alpha-blocker; this prevents reflex tachycardia during alpha-blockade
options.D: Start calcium channel blocker (amlodipine) alone; CCBs are first-line for pheochromocytoma and can be used safely without prior alpha-blockade

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Pheochromocytoma preoperative management — SEQUENCE IS CRITICAL: (1) ALPHA-BLOCKADE FIRST (phenoxybenzamine — irreversible non-selective alpha-blocker; or doxazosin/prazosin — selective alpha-1 blockers) for minimum 10–14 days (ideally 2–4 weeks). Why alpha first: blocks catecholamine-induced vasoconstriction → prevents intraoperative hypertensive crisis when tumor is manipulated. (2) HIGH-SALT DIET + IV FLUIDS to expand intravascular volume (previously contracted due to chronic vasoconstriction — prevents severe hypotension post-tumor removal). (3) BETA-BLOCKER ONLY AFTER alpha-blockade is established (to control reflex tachycardia from alpha-blockade). Why beta AFTER alpha: beta-blocker alone = leaves alpha receptors unopposed → paradoxical hypertension/crisis. Target: BP <130/80, HR 60–80. Incorrect: (A) Surgery without preoperative alpha-blockade = life-threatening hypertensive crisis intraoperatively (can be fatal — surge of catecholamines during tumor manipulation); (C) Beta-blocker FIRST is DANGEROUS in pheo — blocks beta-2 vasodilation leaving alpha vasoconstriction unopposed → hypertensive crisis; (D) CCBs (nicardipine) are used as second-line or adjunct, particularly intraoperatively — NOT as primary preoperative blockade. Exam pearl: Pheo rule: 'ALPHA FIRST, THEN BETA — NEVER BETA FIRST.' Phenoxybenzamine = irreversible alpha blocker (most experience); requires liberal salt/fluid loading. 10% pheo = bilateral, 10% malignant, 10% extra-adrenal (paraganglioma), 10% familial (MEN2, VHL, NF1, SDH mutations).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 32-year-old man presents with recurrent deep vein thrombosis (DVT) — his second episode in 3 years. He is otherwise healthy with no provoking factors. His father also had DVT at age 40. Workup shows: PT normal, aPTT prolonged but corrects with mixing study, anti-cardiolipin antibodies negative, lupus anticoagulant negative, protein C and S normal, AT III normal. Factor V Leiden mutation test is negative. What is the MOST LIKELY diagnosis?

options.A: Factor VIII deficiency (hemophilia A); prolonged aPTT correcting on mixing confirms factor deficiency; factor VIII levels should be checked
options.B: Prothrombin gene mutation (G20210A); causes elevated prothrombin levels and increased thrombotic risk; aPTT prolongation with mixing correction may be seen; autosomal dominant with family history
options.C: Antiphospholipid syndrome; despite negative antibodies, a single negative test is insufficient; repeat testing in 12 weeks
options.D: Protein C deficiency; normal protein C level rules out this diagnosis only in the absence of acute thrombosis or warfarin use

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Prothrombin gene mutation (Factor II G20210A): second most common inherited thrombophilia after Factor V Leiden. Mechanism: point mutation in 3' UTR of prothrombin gene → elevated prothrombin (factor II) levels → increased thrombin generation → thrombophilia. Clinical features: recurrent venous thromboembolism (DVT, PE), family history (autosomal dominant), typically no bleeding (elevated prothrombin = prothrombotic). Lab: aPTT may be slightly prolonged (prothrombin measured in aPTT pathway) — corrects with mixing (factor deficiency pattern, not inhibitor). PT normal. Confirmed by: genetic testing (PCR for G20210A mutation). Factor V Leiden excluded. Incorrect: (A) Hemophilia A = bleeding disorder (hemarthroses, muscle bleeds), X-linked recessive, males affected — does NOT cause thrombosis; elevated factor VIII causes a SHORTENED aPTT (not prolonged); (C) APS requires persistent antibody positivity × 2 (12 weeks apart) — reasonable to recheck, but prothrombin mutation fits better here with family history and negative APS screen; (D) Protein C deficiency causes thrombophilia but protein C was normal — cannot diagnose if normal on testing (caveat: test during acute thrombosis or anticoagulation is unreliable, but clinically this option misdirects). Exam pearl: Inherited thrombophilias: Factor V Leiden (most common, activated protein C resistance), Prothrombin G20210A (2nd most common), AT III deficiency, Protein C deficiency, Protein S deficiency. Long-term anticoagulation in recurrent unprovoked VTE.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 62-year-old retired teacher presents with a 3-year history of resting tremor in the right hand, slowness of movement, and shuffling gait. He noticed micrographia and difficulty turning in bed. Examination shows: pill-rolling tremor at rest (4–5 Hz), cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, and postural instability. His sense of smell has been impaired for 5 years. He has constipation and REM sleep behavior disorder. MoCA score is 24/30. Which feature is MOST INCONSISTENT with idiopathic Parkinson's disease and should prompt investigation for atypical parkinsonism?

options.A: Resting pill-rolling tremor; tremor at rest is the hallmark of Parkinson's disease
options.B: Anosmia preceding motor symptoms by years; Braak staging describes early olfactory bulb involvement in PD
options.C: Severe autonomic failure (orthostatic hypotension causing syncope) as the earliest and most prominent feature from symptom onset, with minimal tremor
options.D: Mild cognitive impairment (MoCA 24); slight cognitive decline is common in early PD and does not suggest atypical parkinsonism

questions.explanation: Correct (C): This question asks what is INCONSISTENT with IDIOPATHIC PD (i.e., suggests atypical parkinsonism/Parkinson-plus syndrome). Atypical parkinsonism red flags: (1) Early prominent autonomic failure (syncope, severe OH from onset) = Multiple System Atrophy (MSA-P); (2) Early falls/postural instability within 1 year of onset = PSP (Progressive Supranuclear Palsy); (3) Vertical gaze palsy (downgaze) = PSP; (4) Poor/absent levodopa response; (5) Rapid progression; (6) Cerebellar signs; (7) Early severe dementia (within 1 year) = DLB or CBD. MSA features: severe early autonomic failure (OH, urinary incontinence, ED), cerebellar ataxia, minimal tremor, poor levodopa response. Typical PD features (all present in this patient): resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, asymmetric onset, anosmia (Braak stage 1–2), constipation, REM sleep behavior disorder (prodromal PD features), mild cognitive impairment. Incorrect: (A) Resting tremor IS a hallmark of PD — consistent, not concerning for atypical; (B) Anosmia preceding motor symptoms = Braak staging (PD starts in olfactory bulb/lower brainstem) — supports PD; (D) Mild cognitive impairment in early PD is common (PD-MCI); dementia developing >1 year after motor onset = PDD (Parkinson's disease dementia) — consistent with PD. Exam pearl: PSP red flags: 'FALLS first, DOWNWARD gaze palsy, EARLY dementia, AXIAL > appendicular rigidity.' MSA: 'Autonomic + Cerebellar/Parkinsonism, poor levodopa response, atrophy on MRI (putamen, pons, cerebellum).' DLB: dementia BEFORE or within 1 year of parkinsonism.

questions.image_title: HRCT chest showing honeycombing with basal predominance
key_findings: Bilateral basal and peripheral predominant honeycombing
Traction bronchiectasis within areas of fibrosis
Subpleural distribution of fibrotic changes
Ground-glass opacity less prominent than fibrosis
No upper lobe predominance or centrilobular nodules
Absence of lymphadenopathy or pleural effusion
questions.question_text: A 68-year-old male ex-smoker presents with 2 years of progressive exertional dyspnea and dry cough. Examination reveals bilateral basal Velcro-like crackles and finger clubbing. PFT shows FVC 62% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.82 (preserved ratio), DLCO 48% predicted. The HRCT chest is shown. Multidisciplinary team (MDT) agrees on a diagnosis of Usual Interstitial Pneumonia (UIP) pattern — consistent with IPF. Which of the following represents the MOST APPROPRIATE disease-modifying treatment?

options.A: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day + azathioprine + NAC triple therapy; this combination was proven superior in the PANTHER-IPF trial
options.B: Nintedanib (tyrosine kinase inhibitor) or pirfenidone (anti-fibrotic); both slow disease progression (reduce FVC decline) in IPF; choice based on side-effect profile and patient preference
options.C: Cyclophosphamide + methylprednisolone pulse; aggressive immunosuppression is needed for rapidly progressive IPF
options.D: Azithromycin long-term therapy; macrolide anti-inflammatory effects reduce fibrosis progression in IPF similar to bronchiectasis

questions.explanation: Correct (B): IPF (Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis) — UIP pattern on HRCT (honeycombing + traction bronchiectasis, basal peripheral predominant) is diagnostic. Disease-modifying antifibrotic drugs: (1) NINTEDANIB (INPULSIS trial): tyrosine kinase inhibitor (VEGFR, FGFR, PDGFR) → reduces FVC decline by ~50%; GI side effects (diarrhea); (2) PIRFENIDONE (ASCEND, CAPACITY trials): anti-fibrotic, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant → reduces FVC decline; side effects: photosensitivity, GI, fatigue. Both are approved for mild-moderate IPF (FVC >50%, DLCO >30%). Lung transplantation for advanced disease. Pulmonary rehab improves QOL. Incorrect: (A) PANTHER-IPF trial: triple therapy (prednisone + azathioprine + NAC) showed INCREASED hospitalizations and mortality compared to placebo — trial stopped early; this combination is CONTRAINDICATED in IPF; (C) IPF is a fibrotic (not inflammatory) condition — aggressive immunosuppression is HARMFUL (increases infections, no antifibrotic effect); (D) Macrolides have no evidence for antifibrotic benefit in IPF; used in bronchiectasis and COPD for anti-inflammatory effects but not IPF. Exam pearl: IPF = fibrosis, NOT inflammation — do NOT use steroids/immunosuppressants. Antifibrotics slow but do not reverse. Acute exacerbation of IPF: dramatic worsening over days-weeks despite treatment → poor prognosis. DLCO most sensitive PFT parameter in ILD. IPF prognosis: median survival 3–5 years from diagnosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old male known HIV-positive patient (not on ART) presents with 3 weeks of subacute headache, low-grade fever, and mild confusion. CD4 count is 52 cells/μL. CSF analysis: opening pressure 32 cmH2O, WBC 12 (lymphocytic), protein 68 mg/dL, glucose 32 mg/dL (serum glucose 90). India ink preparation of CSF is positive. CSF cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) is positive at titre 1:512. What is the MOST APPROPRIATE antifungal regimen for induction therapy?

options.A: Fluconazole 400 mg/day for 8 weeks; it is the preferred induction agent for cryptococcal meningitis due to superior CNS penetration
options.B: Amphotericin B deoxycholate (0.7–1 mg/kg/day IV) + flucytosine (25 mg/kg QID) for 2 weeks (induction); followed by fluconazole 400 mg/day for 8 weeks (consolidation); then fluconazole 200 mg/day for at least 1 year (maintenance)
options.C: Voriconazole 6 mg/kg BD × 2 doses then 4 mg/kg BD; voriconazole has superior activity against Cryptococcus compared to amphotericin
options.D: Micafungin IV + fluconazole oral combination; echinocandins are first-line for CNS fungal infections in immunocompromised patients

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Cryptococcal meningitis in HIV (WHO/IDSA guidelines): INDUCTION (2 weeks): Amphotericin B deoxycholate 0.7–1 mg/kg/day IV + Flucytosine (5-FC) 25 mg/kg QID PO. Combination superior to Ampho B alone (significantly reduces mortality — IDSA/WHO ACTA trial). If flucytosine unavailable: AmB + fluconazole 800 mg/day. Liposomal AmB (3–4 mg/kg/day) preferred if renal impairment. CONSOLIDATION (8 weeks): Fluconazole 400 mg/day. MAINTENANCE (≥1 year): Fluconazole 200 mg/day until CD4 >200 × 2 readings on ART. Elevated ICP management: serial lumbar punctures (reduce opening pressure) or lumbar drain — critical to prevent blindness and death. ART: start 4–6 weeks after antifungal initiation (not immediately — IRIS risk with fungal meningitis can be fatal). Incorrect: (A) Fluconazole ALONE as induction = inferior (higher mortality, slower sterilization); used only if AmB unavailable; (C) Voriconazole = NOT active against Cryptococcus; used for Aspergillus and some Candida species; (D) Echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin) have NO activity against Cryptococcus — Cryptococcus lacks glucan synthase target (primary echinocandin target). Exam pearl: Amphotericin + 5-FC = gold standard for cryptococcal induction. 5-FC side effects: bone marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity — monitor blood counts. India ink = 'halo/capsule' around yeast. CrAg = most sensitive test. Opening pressure >25 cmH2O = increased ICP — aggressive LP management critical.

questions.question_text: A 70-year-old woman on hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension presents with nausea, headache, and confusion. Serum sodium is 118 mEq/L. She has no edema, JVP is normal, and skin turgor is reduced. Urine sodium is 45 mEq/L and urine osmolality is 480 mOsm/kg. Serum osmolality is 245 mOsm/kg. What is the MOST APPROPRIATE rate of correction of hyponatremia in this chronic setting?

options.A: Correct sodium rapidly at 2–3 mEq/L/hour with 3% NaCl until symptoms resolve completely; speed of correction is the priority in symptomatic hyponatremia
options.B: Correct sodium at no more than 8–10 mEq/L in 24 hours (maximum 18 mEq/L in 48 hours); overcorrection causes osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS/central pontine myelinolysis)
options.C: Restrict water to 500 mL/day; water restriction alone is adequate for thiazide-induced hyponatremia regardless of symptom severity
options.D: Give IV 0.9% normal saline at 250 mL/hour; isotonic saline corrects hyponatremia most safely by diluting the hypertonic urine

questions.explanation: Correct (B): This is CHRONIC hyponatremia (>48 hours — onset unknown/insidious in elderly patient on thiazide) with neurological symptoms (confusion). Thiazide mechanism: blocks NaCl cotransporter in distal tubule → cannot dilute urine → water retention → hyponatremia with high urine osmolality and high urine Na (SIADH-like picture but thiazide-induced). Correction rate: CHRONIC hyponatremia — brain has adapted (volume regulation) — rapid correction causes osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS/CPM) — demyelination of pons → locked-in syndrome, quadriplegia, dysarthria, death. Safe correction rate: 6–8 mEq/L per 24 hours (maximum 10 mEq/L in first 24 hours; 18 mEq in 48 hours). STOP thiazide; give isotonic fluids cautiously; if severe/seizures: 3% NaCl 1–2 mL/kg/hr (bolus 100–150 mL) to raise Na by 4–6 mEq/L, then switch to slower correction. Monitor Na every 2–4 hours. Incorrect: (A) 2–3 mEq/L/hour is too rapid for chronic hyponatremia — causes ODS; this rate is for acute (<48 hours) severe symptomatic only; (C) Water restriction alone is appropriate for asymptomatic/mild; confusion requires active treatment; (D) Isotonic saline may actually worsen hyponatremia in SIADH-like states (high urine osmolality — kidneys retain water and excrete Na from NS → worsens dilutional hyponatremia). Exam pearl: ODS/CPM risk: alcoholism, malnutrition, chronic hyponatremia. 'Correct SLOWLY: 6–8 mEq/L per day maximum.' Rapid correction after adaptation = osmotic injury to myelin sheaths.

questions.question_text: A 64-year-old man with known ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 35%) is brought to the emergency with palpitations and mild dizziness for 2 hours. BP is 104/68 mmHg. The ECG shown above demonstrates a wide complex tachycardia. Which single finding on this ECG is MOST diagnostic of ventricular tachycardia over SVT with aberrancy?

options.A: Heart rate of 180 bpm with regular rhythm
options.B: AV dissociation with fusion beats
options.C: QRS duration greater than 140 ms
options.D: Left axis deviation on the tracing

questions.explanation: Correct (B): AV dissociation (P waves marching independently through QRS complexes) with fusion beats (Dressler beats — partial capture of ventricle by sinus impulse merging with VT) is PATHOGNOMONIC of ventricular tachycardia. This finding is present in ~25% of VT cases but when present, it unambiguously confirms VT. Fusion and capture beats are diagnostic because they can only occur when there are two independent ventricular activation sources (sinus + ectopic ventricular focus). Brugada criteria (1991) and Vereckei criteria rely on multiple ECG features. Incorrect: (A) Rate of 180 bpm does not differentiate — both VT and SVT with aberrancy can occur at this rate; (C) QRS >140 ms in RBBB morphology or >160 ms in LBBB morphology favors VT but is not diagnostic alone — aberrant conduction in SVT also produces wide QRS; (D) Left axis deviation is a supportive criterion in Brugada algorithm but not diagnostic by itself — inferior MI causing axis deviation can exist alongside SVT. Exam Pearl: In any patient with structural heart disease + wide complex tachycardia → treat as VT until proven otherwise. Mnemonic for VT: 'ABCDE' — AV dissociation, Broad QRS >160ms, Concordance in precordial leads, Dominant R in aVR, Every beat is regular.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 62-year-old male ex-smoker presents with progressive breathlessness over 18 months and a non-productive cough. Examination reveals bilateral fine basal crepitations and finger clubbing. PFTs show FVC 58% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.82, DLCO 42% predicted. HRCT chest shows bilateral basal predominant subpleural honeycombing with traction bronchiectasis. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows no predominant cell type. Surgical lung biopsy demonstrates fibroblastic foci, temporal heterogeneity, and UIP pattern. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Start high-dose prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day and reassess after 3 months
options.B: Initiate nintedanib or pirfenidone and refer for lung transplant evaluation
options.C: Prescribe N-acetylcysteine triple therapy and supplemental oxygen
options.D: Perform repeat HRCT in 6 months before initiating any treatment

questions.explanation: Correct (B): This is a classic presentation of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) — UIP pattern on HRCT + biopsy with fibroblastic foci and temporal heterogeneity. The two approved antifibrotic agents are: (1) Nintedanib (INPULSIS trial) — tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting PDGFR, FGFR, VEGFR; reduces annual FVC decline by ~50%; (2) Pirfenidone (ASCEND trial) — reduces TGF-β mediated fibrosis; also reduces FVC decline. Both are recommended in international guidelines (ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT 2022). Lung transplant evaluation should be initiated early given FVC <60% and DLCO <40%. Incorrect: (A) Corticosteroids are NOT recommended in IPF — the PANTHER-IPF trial showed triple therapy (prednisone + azathioprine + NAC) caused INCREASED hospitalizations and mortality; IPF is a fibrotic, not inflammatory process; (C) N-acetylcysteine monotherapy showed no benefit (PANTHER-IPF NAC arm); (D) Watchful waiting is inappropriate — disease is progressive with poor prognosis (median survival 3-5 years); delaying antifibrotic therapy worsens outcomes. Exam Pearl: IPF = UIP on HRCT + exclusion of other causes. Key HRCT: bilateral basal subpleural honeycombing ± traction bronchiectasis. DO NOT give steroids. Give antifibrotics + transplant referral. DLCO is the most sensitive PFT marker for ILD.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 44-year-old woman is admitted with fever, oliguria, and a maculopapular rash 3 weeks after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a UTI. Investigations: Serum creatinine 3.8 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL), BUN 58 mg/dL, serum eosinophils 12%, urine eosinophils positive, urine sodium 52 mEq/L, urine osmolality 310 mOsm/kg, FENa 3.2%. Renal biopsy shows diffuse interstitial infiltration with lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils with relative sparing of glomeruli. Which statement BEST describes the pathophysiology and expected course of this condition?

options.A: Immune complex deposition in glomerular basement membrane causing membranous nephropathy; will not recover without dialysis
options.B: Drug-induced T-cell mediated hypersensitivity targeting tubular antigens causing acute interstitial nephritis; recovery expected after drug withdrawal ± steroids
options.C: Direct tubular toxicity by sulfonamide metabolites causing acute tubular necrosis; recovery depends on hydration status alone
options.D: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation in renal vasculature causing cortical ischemia; requires antihistamine therapy

questions.explanation: Correct (B): This is classic Drug-Induced Acute Interstitial Nephritis (AIN) caused by TMP-SMX. Pathophysiology: Type IV (T-cell mediated delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction where drug acts as a hapten, triggering CD4+ T-cell activation → tubular antigen-directed inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils). Key features: (1) Triad: fever + rash + eosinophilia (only in ~10-30% of cases); (2) Urine eosinophils (Hansel stain — though sensitivity ~67%); (3) Intrinsic renal failure: high FENa (>2%), high urine Na, low urine osmolality; (4) Biopsy: interstitial infiltrate with eosinophils ± tubulitis. Management: Stop offending drug → 60-70% recover baseline function; if no recovery in 5-7 days or severe AKI → short course prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day for 4 weeks then taper). Incorrect: (A) Membranous nephropathy presents with nephrotic syndrome, not AIN pattern; immunofluorescence shows granular IgG + C3; (C) ATN shows muddy brown granular casts, not eosinophilic infiltrate; direct toxicity doesn't produce rash/eosinophilia; (D) IgE-mediated reactions are Type I — anaphylaxis, not AIN. Exam Pearl: TMP-SMX, NSAIDs, PPIs, beta-lactams = most common drugs causing AIN. NSAIDs also cause minimal change disease (concurrent with AIN). FENa >2% = intrinsic renal failure. Biopsy gold standard.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old woman in her 12th week of first pregnancy presents for routine antenatal screening. She is clinically euthyroid. Labs show: TSH 0.2 mIU/L (normal in pregnancy: 0.1–2.5 mIU/L in first trimester), Free T4 14 pmol/L (normal), anti-TPO antibodies negative, beta-hCG 198,000 IU/L. She has no previous thyroid history. What is the MOST APPROPRIATE management?

options.A: Start propylthiouracil immediately to prevent fetal thyrotoxicosis
options.B: No treatment required; gestational transient thyrotoxicosis due to hCG cross-reactivity with TSH receptor
options.C: Order thyroid uptake scan to rule out Graves' disease before deciding treatment
options.D: Start carbimazole 10 mg/day as TSH suppression indicates subclinical hyperthyroidism requiring treatment

questions.explanation: Correct (B): This is Gestational Transient Thyrotoxicosis (GTT) — a physiological phenomenon unique to pregnancy. Mechanism: hCG shares structural homology with TSH (both are glycoprotein hormones with identical alpha subunits) and has weak TSH-receptor agonist activity. In the first trimester, extremely high hCG levels (peaks at 10-12 weeks) cause TSH suppression and mild FT4 elevation. Diagnosis: suppressed TSH + normal/mildly elevated FT4 + high hCG + negative anti-TPO + anti-TSH receptor antibodies + clinically euthyroid + no goiter. Management: No antithyroid drugs — condition resolves spontaneously by 14-18 weeks as hCG declines. Monitor TFTs in 4-6 weeks. Incorrect: (A) PTU causes agranulocytosis, hepatotoxicity (black box warning — liver failure); contraindicated unless overt hyperthyroidism with TSH-receptor antibodies confirmed; (C) Radioiodine scan is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy — fetal thyroid ablation risk; (D) Subclinical hyperthyroidism in pregnancy does not require antithyroid therapy — only overt hyperthyroidism (TSH <0.1 + elevated FT4 + symptoms + positive TRAb) is treated, preferably with PTU in first trimester, carbimazole from second trimester. Exam Pearl: GTT vs Graves' in pregnancy: GTT = high hCG + negative TRAb + no goiter + resolves by 18 weeks. Graves' = positive TRAb + goiter + persists. NEVER give radioiodine in pregnancy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 24-year-old woman with known SLE (on hydroxychloroquine) presents with worsening headache, confusion, and a seizure. BP is 178/112 mmHg. Labs: Hb 7.2 g/dL, platelets 34,000/mm³, serum creatinine 2.9 mg/dL (baseline 0.8), LDH 890 IU/L, peripheral smear shows schistocytes. Urine: proteinuria 3+, RBC casts. Anti-dsDNA titer is markedly elevated (480 IU/mL, prev 40). Complement C3 is low. Which of the following best explains this clinical picture, and what is the MOST urgent treatment?

options.A: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) triggered by SLE flare; urgent plasma exchange is the treatment of choice
options.B: Lupus nephritis Class IV + Neuropsychiatric SLE flare; pulse methylprednisolone + cyclophosphamide is indicated
options.C: Antiphospholipid syndrome with CAPS; anticoagulation with heparin + steroids is most urgent
options.D: Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) from SLE-associated complement dysregulation; eculizumab is first-line therapy

questions.explanation: Correct (B): This presentation represents a severe SLE flare with two major organ threats: (1) Lupus Nephritis Class IV (diffuse proliferative — most severe): active urine sediment (RBC casts, heavy proteinuria), AKI, elevated anti-dsDNA, low complement → typical of immune complex-mediated glomerulonephritis in SLE; (2) Neuropsychiatric SLE (NPSLE): seizure + confusion + hypertension in the setting of severe flare. Management: IV pulse methylprednisolone 1g/day × 3 days → followed by high-dose oral prednisone + cyclophosphamide (NIH regimen for Class IV LN — MAINTAIN trial) OR mycophenolate mofetil (ALMS trial showed equivalence). Belimumab/voclosporin can be added. Incorrect: (A) TTP (Moschcowitz syndrome) should be considered in MAHA + thrombocytopenia, but in SLE context with active sediment + elevated anti-dsDNA + low complement → SLE flare is primary diagnosis; ADAMTS-13 activity <10% would confirm TTP — plasma exchange holds if TTP cannot be excluded but LN treatment takes priority here; (C) CAPS (Catastrophic APS) requires positive APL antibodies + multi-organ thrombosis; this picture fits active SLE flare better than CAPS; (D) Eculizumab (complement C5 inhibitor) is used for atypical HUS with complement dysregulation — not first-line for SLE nephritis. Exam Pearl: Anti-dsDNA + low C3/C4 = active SLE nephritis. RBC casts = glomerulonephritis. Class IV LN = most common severe lupus nephritis; treat with steroids + cyclophosphamide or MMF. SLEDAI score guides disease activity.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 52-year-old male with alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD 22) presents with increased abdominal girth. Paracentesis reveals: total protein 1.2 g/dL, LDH 85 IU/L, glucose 98 mg/dL, SAAG 1.8 g/dL, cell count 180 cells/mm³ (90% lymphocytes, 10% neutrophils). PMN count is 80/mm³. He is hemodynamically stable. Which statement regarding management is MOST accurate?

options.A: PMN count 80/mm³ meets criteria for SBP; start cefotaxime 2g IV q8h immediately
options.B: SAAG ≥1.1 confirms portal hypertensive ascites; prescribe spironolactone + furosemide; no antibiotics indicated
options.C: Lymphocyte-predominant exudate suggests tuberculous peritonitis; initiate empiric anti-TB therapy
options.D: Low protein ascites with high SAAG indicates chylous ascites; dietary fat restriction is primary management

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Analysis of this ascitic fluid: SAAG 1.8 g/dL (≥1.1 = portal hypertension — 97% accuracy; causes include cirrhosis, cardiac ascites, Budd-Chiari, massive liver mets). Total protein <2.5 g/dL (low protein) + high SAAG = classic cirrhotic ascites. PMN count = 80/mm³ — SBP diagnosis requires PMN ≥250/mm³; this patient does NOT meet SBP criteria. Cell count 180/mm³ with predominantly lymphocytes is a non-specific mild pleocytosis. Management: First-line for cirrhotic ascites = sodium restriction (<2 g/day) + diuretics: spironolactone (100 mg/day, max 400 mg) + furosemide (40 mg/day, max 160 mg) in 100:40 ratio to maintain normokalemia. Incorrect: (A) SBP requires PMN ≥250/mm³ — this patient has PMN 80/mm³, which does NOT meet the threshold; starting antibiotics without indication risks C. difficile and antibiotic resistance; (C) TB peritonitis typically shows: high protein (exudate >2.5 g/dL), low SAAG (<1.1 g/dL), lymphocyte predominance, high ADA; this patient has high SAAG (portal HTN pattern), not consistent with TB; (D) Chylous ascites: milky appearance, triglycerides >200 mg/dL, caused by lymphatic obstruction (lymphoma, trauma, post-surgical); this doesn't fit the picture. Exam Pearl: SAAG ≥1.1 = portal hypertension (97% accuracy). SBP: PMN ≥250/mm³ → treat without waiting for culture. Most common organism in SBP = E. coli. Prophylaxis: norfloxacin 400 mg/day for secondary prophylaxis after first SBP episode.
